activities.anchor: By 1907 Europe was divided into two fortified camps
activities.caption: file each fact — safety net or tripwire?
activities.name: wwAllianceBuckets

config.prompt: The alliance system — file each fact:

items.label: for forty years the balance helped keep the great-power peace
an aggressor would face two fronts, so partners could restrain a threatened power
any local quarrel could drag in an ally — no quarrel so small
the alliances were secret or vague, so each government hedged with more arms
the Anglo-German naval race after HMS Dreadnought (1906)
standing armies that nearly doubled in size between 1870 and 1914

config.why: The honest answer is both, in different ways — crises over Morocco (1905, 1911) and the Balkans were defused for decades, and then the tripwire fired.

config.prompt: From one murder to a world war — order the steps, earliest first:
items: 28 June — Franz Ferdinand shot in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip
23 July — Austria-Hungary issues Serbia an ultimatum designed to be refused
28 July — Austria declares war on Serbia
1 August — Germany declares war on Russia, which had mobilised to defend Serbia
3 August — Germany declares war on France
4 August — Germany invades Belgium, bringing Britain in
config.why: Five weeks — each step locally 'logical', collectively catastrophic. Mobilisation timetables removed the last room for hesitation, and the alliance system converted a Balkan duel into a general war.

activities.caption: pair each reason with its mechanism
activities.name: wwEmpireMatch

config.prompt: Empire as engine of tension — pair each reason with its mechanism:

pairs.right: a great power, by definition, had colonies — Germany demanded its 'place in the sun'
raw materials, captive markets and investment outlets — the feedstock of pre-war protectionism
every new colonial boundary a potential flashpoint between powers
compromise each time — and each side more convinced the other was encircling it

config.why: Colonial competition did not cause the war of 1914 directly — the trigger was European — but it normalised rivalry and armed it.

activities.anchor: New weapons — machine guns, heavy artillery, poison gas, tanks, aircraft
activities.caption: call the toll — the first day of the Somme
activities.name: wwSommeEstimate

config.prompt: The Somme's first day (1 July 1916) cost Britain roughly how many casualties?
config.why: 57,000 on the first day; the battle eventually killed or wounded over a million men for a few miles — and around 10 million soldiers died in the war as a whole.
config.context: New weapons met nineteenth-century tactics, and the Western Front congealed into trenches from Switzerland to the Channel.

activities.anchor: The peacemakers also redrew eastern Europe
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the peace that failed
activities.name: wwVersaillesSpot

config.prompt: One line of this Versailles briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: Germany lost about 13% of its territory, all its colonies and its navy.
Article 231 assigned war guilt as the basis for reparations set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.
Germany was dismembered and permanently occupied.
Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia were created on the nationality principle, with millions of minorities on the 'wrong' side of each border.
The League of Nations lacked the United States, whose Senate refused to join.
config.correction: Germany was punished just enough to be enraged and not enough to be disabled — it was neither dismembered nor permanently occupied, the worst of both worlds.
config.why: Keynes, present at the conference, predicted the terms would poison European recovery — and the Second World War grew in the cracks Versailles left.

activities.anchor: tried to satisfy the revisionists cheaply
activities.caption: the Cabinet's dilemma, 1936–39 — decide
activities.name: wwMunichBranch

config.root: You advise the British Cabinet between 1936 and 1939. Each move has a price — decide.

start.text: Hitler remilitarises the Rhineland (1936) — a treaty violation with an army behind it.

choices.label: Confront Germany now
choices.feedback: The cabinet table is unmoved — the country is scarred by 1914–18, preoccupied by empire and Depression.

choices.label: Let it pass — challenge later
choices.feedback: The crises keep coming: Japan had seized Manchuria (1931), Italy Abyssinia (1935–36), and Germany annexed Austria in March 1938.

confront.text: There is no coalition willing to fight, and the rearmament race has barely begun.

choices.label: Continue to September 1938
choices.feedback: By then Germany has annexed Austria — and demands the Czech Sudetenland.

munich.text: Munich, September 1938: hand over the Sudetenland in exchange for peace promises — or refuse and draw the line now?

choices.label: Hand over the Sudetenland
choices.feedback: The promises lasted barely six months.

choices.label: Refuse — draw the line now
choices.feedback: The road actually taken reversed only after the rest of Czechoslovakia fell in March 1939 — the counterfactual historians still argue.

handover.text: March 1939: Germany invades the rest of Czechoslovakia. The policy finally reverses — guarantees to Poland.

choices.label: Guarantee Poland and mean it
choices.feedback: When Hitler invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, Britain and France declared war on 3 September.

refuse.text: A standoff at Munich. One fact in your files: German rearmament was far from ready in 1938 — a discovery made only after 1945, which keeps the 'did it buy a year?' argument alive.

end.text: The war comes either way; the argument is over whether the year was bought or thrown away.

config.why: The verdict of folly rests on what Munich taught Hitler, not on what Chamberlain knew.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — which front decided it?
activities.name: wwEasternPredict

config.q: Where was the war in Europe actually decided?
choices: The Western Front — D-Day decided it
The Eastern Front — about four of every five German soldiers who died in the whole war died there, and Stalingrad ended more than a year before Normandy
config.why: D-Day hastened the end; it did not decide it. The Eastern Front was the war's centre of gravity, and the Soviet Union paid for the victory with roughly 27 million dead.

activities.name: wwLegacyCloze

config.text: The %%0%% (1945) replaced the League with great-power vetoes; the Nuremberg trials established that '%%1%%' is not a defence and invented the crime of crimes against humanity; and the atomic bomb split war itself in two.
